verdicts.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/raspberry-pi-os.md (fetched 2026-10-09). The heading is 'Install Docker Engine on Raspberry Pi OS (32-bit / armhf)'. The warning reads word for word: 'Docker Engine v28 will be the last major version to support Raspberry Pi OS 32-bit (armhf). Starting with Docker Engine v29, new major versions will no longer provide packages for Raspberry Pi OS 32-bit (armhf).' Migration options: '64-bit ARM: Install the Debian `arm64` packages (fully supported)' and '32-bit ARM (v7): Install the Debian `armhf` packages (targets ARMv7 CPUs)'. It adds: 'Older devices based on the ARMv6 architecture are no longer supported by official packages, including: Raspberry Pi 1 (Model A/B/A+/B+), Raspberry Pi Zero and Zero W'. Caveat: only arm64 is called 'fully supported'; armhf on Pi OS gets no support statement. The same page still tells you to add .../linux/raspbian, and its example output shows '5:29.8.2-1~raspbian.12~bookworm'. That version string is a docs template: no such package exists in the repo (see DOCKER-03), so pinning VERSION_STRING as the page shows would fail.

https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/29.md, section '## 29.0.0' dated 2025-11-10, under 'Breaking Changes': 'Debian armhf (32-bit) packages now target ARMv7 CPUs and will not work on ARMv6 devices.' and 'Official Raspbian (32-bit) packages are no longer provided. Use Debian arm64 packages for 64-bit devices, or Debian armhf packages for 32-bit ARMv7 devices.' The same section also has 'The daemon now requires API version `v1.44` or later' and 'cgroup v1 is deprecated'.

curl https://download.docker.com/linux/raspbian/dists/ (2026-10-09) lists bookworm/, bullseye/, buster/, jessie/ and stretch/; there is no trixie. In dists/bookworm/pool/stable/armhf/ the newest docker-ce is docker-ce_28.5.2-1~raspbian.12~bookworm_armhf.deb (2025-11-05 15:28:15) and there are no 29.x files. https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/28.md lists '## 28.5.2' (2025-11-05) as the newest 28.x, and the Debian repo's 28.x line also ends at 28.5.2. Nuance on 'frozen': the docker-ce engine stopped at 28.5.2, but other packages kept updating for three more months: containerd.io_2.2.1 (2026-01-02), docker-compose-plugin 5.0.2 (2026-01-21), docker-buildx-plugin 0.31.1 (2026-01-29) and docker-model-plugin 1.0.12 (2026-02-12). dists/bookworm/Release is dated 'Thu, 12 Feb 2026'. Nothing has changed since, so containerd.io there is stuck at 2.2.1 while the Debian repo has 2.3.6.

Directory listings fetched 2026-10-09. download.docker.com/linux/debian/dists/trixie/pool/stable/armhf/ has docker-ce_29.8.2-1~debian.13~trixie_armhf.deb (2026-09-30 19:54:48) and containerd.io_2.3.6-1~debian.13~trixie_armhf.deb (2026-09-25). .../trixie/pool/stable/arm64/ has docker-ce 29.8.2 (2026-09-30 19:54:58) and containerd.io 2.3.6. .../bookworm/pool/stable/armhf/ and .../bookworm/pool/stable/arm64/ also have docker-ce 29.8.2 (2026-09-30) and containerd.io 2.3.6 (2026-09-25). https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian.md lists 'Debian Trixie 13 (stable)' and 'Debian Bookworm 12 (oldstable)', and says 'Docker Engine for Debian is compatible with x86_64 (or amd64), armhf (arm/v7), arm64, and ppc64le (ppc64el) architectures.' The page says 'compatible with', not 'supports'. The 29.8.2 section of the 29 release notes is dated 2026-09-30.

https://get.docker.com/ (fetched 2026-10-09) contains SCRIPT_COMMIT_SHA="2b32480025b223ebfddae9a3a8bef09027680f53". Apart from that SHA line it is identical to https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docker/docker-install/master/install.sh. Lines 589-596: 'apt_repo_lsb_dist="$lsb_dist"  # Docker does not publish a Raspbian Trixie repo; use Debian Trixie instead.  if [ "$lsb_dist" = "raspbian" ] && [ "$dist_version" = "trixie" ]; then apt_repo_lsb_dist="debian"', then 'apt_repo="deb [...] $DOWNLOAD_URL/linux/$apt_repo_lsb_dist $dist_version $CHANNEL"'. So raspbian/bookworm still gets '/linux/raspbian bookworm stable'. The deprecation case lists only 'raspbian.buster|raspbian.stretch|raspbian.jessie'; raspbian.bullseye and raspbian.bookworm get no notice. dist_version is derived from /etc/debian_version (13 -> trixie, 12 -> bookworm).

verdicts.corrected_claim: Restart policies have no post-stop hook. moby#28837 ('Proposal: support custom hooks (prestart, poststart, poststop)') is a community proposal, not one from Docker, and it is closed as not planned. Docker's docs say verbatim 'Docker recommends that you use restart policies, and avoid using process managers to start containers' and warn 'Don't combine Docker restart policies with host-level process managers, as this creates conflicts.' However, a systemd unit wrapping the docker CLI with ExecStopPost= is NOT the only way to get a host-side GPIO reset. CDI is enabled by default since Docker 28.2.0. A root-owned CDI spec in /etc/cdi (which can also inject /dev/gpiochip*) may declare an OCI 'poststop' hook. Docker's CDI injection adds it to the OCI spec, dockerd deletes the task on every container exit before it evaluates the restart policy, and runc's destroy() runs poststop hooks on the host. This should give a pin reset after every container exit, including kill -9, even with restart policies. This is inferred from source code and not tested on a Pi. If you do use a systemd unit wrapping the CLI, Docker's docs say to use 'the same `docker start` or `docker service` command'. systemd then supervises only the CLI client, not the container (see missed).
verdicts.evidence: https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/start-containers-automatically.md: 'Docker recommends that you use restart policies, and avoid using process managers to start containers.'; '> Don't combine Docker restart policies with host-level process managers, as this creates conflicts.'; 'configure it to start your container or service using the same `docker start` or `docker service` command you would normally use'. https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/28837: title 'Proposal: support custom hooks (prestart, poststart, poststop)', page shows 'Closed as not planned' (stateReason NOT_PLANNED). CDI hooks: https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/28.md, section 28.2.0: 'CDI is now enabled by default. moby/moby#49963'. CDI SPEC.md (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cncf-tags/container-device-interface/main/SPEC.md): hookName 'should be one of {createRuntime, createContainer, startContainer, poststart, poststop}'. CDI library pkg/cdi/container-edits.go: 'case PoststopHook: editor.AddPostStopHook(ociHook)'. moby daemon/cdi.go injectCDIDevices calls 'c.registry.InjectDevices(s, cdiDeviceNames...)'. moby daemon/monitor.go handleContainerExit calls 'es, err := tsk.Delete(ctx)' before 'c.RestartManager().ShouldRestart(...)'. runc libcontainer/state_linux.go destroy() calls 'err := runPoststopHooks(c)', which runs 'hooks.Run(configs.Poststop, s)'.

I downloaded docker-ce_29.8.2-1~debian.13~trixie_arm64.deb and extracted /usr/lib/systemd/system/docker.service. It contains 'After=network-online.target nss-lookup.target docker.socket firewalld.service containerd.service time-set.target', 'Wants=network-online.target containerd.service', 'Requires=docker.socket', 'StartLimitBurst=3', 'StartLimitIntervalSec=60', 'Type=notify', 'TimeoutStartSec=0', 'Restart=always' and 'KillMode=process'. diff against https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/master/contrib/init/systemd/docker.service: identical. How long the delay is depends on the system. The unit uses Wants=, not Requires=, so dockerd still starts if the network never comes up. On a NetworkManager system (Pi OS since Bookworm), NetworkManager-wait-online.service has 'ExecStart=@bindir@/nm-online -s -q' and 'Environment=NM_ONLINE_TIMEOUT=60', which waits up to about 60 s when no network is available (https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/NetworkManager/NetworkManager/-/raw/main/data/NetworkManager-wait-online.service.in). systemd.special(7) says time-set.target 'is typically not delayed by network problems'. The delay itself is still not measured.

https://docs.docker.com/engine/daemon/live-restore.md: 'By default, when the Docker daemon terminates, it shuts down running containers.' and '[live restore] is only supported when installing patch releases (`YY.MM.x`), not for major (`YY.MM`) daemon upgrades. If you skip releases during an upgrade, the daemon may not restore its connection to the containers'. The package upgrade path is confirmed in the 29.8.2 docker-ce .deb postinst (dh_installsystemd): 'if [ -n "$2" ]; then _dh_action=restart ... deb-systemd-invoke $_dh_action 'docker.service' 'docker.socket''. So every apt upgrade of docker-ce restarts dockerd, which stops the controller container unless live-restore is set. Even with live-restore, a major upgrade is not covered. Restart-policy containers come back after the daemon restarts, but the in-progress brew is interrupted.

https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall.md: '> The `docker` group grants root-level privileges to the user.' and 'A group password reduces ambient access to the Docker socket, but it doesn't reduce the root-level privileges granted after access is authorized.' https://docs.docker.com/engine/security.md, 'Docker daemon attack surface': 'This daemon requires `root` privileges unless you opt-in to Rootless mode' and 'First of all, only trusted users should be allowed to control your Docker daemon. This is a direct consequence of some powerful Docker features. Specifically, Docker allows you to share a directory between the Docker host and a guest container ... without limiting the access rights of the container.'

verdicts.corrected_claim: Watchtower is unmaintained. containrrr/watchtower was archived on 2025-12-17, and its README says 'This project is no longer maintained' and points to Discussion #2135 ('Goodbye containrrr/watchtower!', 2025-12-17). The maintainers advise against using any of the forks. Its last release is v1.7.1 (2023-11-11). With default settings it fails against Docker 29 because it pins DOCKER_API_VERSION=1.25 by default. On 29.0.0 (issue #2126, 2025-11-14) the error was 'client version 1.25 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.44'. Docker 29.3.0 (2026-03-05) lowered the daemon minimum to v1.40, which is still above 1.25, so it still fails, but setting DOCKER_API_VERSION to 1.40 or higher works around it. Standalone Docker containers have no built-in update-with-rollback. Swarm-mode services do (`docker service update --update-failure-action rollback`), but `docker service create` has no --device option, so swarm services cannot be given /dev/gpiochip* and swarm is not usable here.
verdicts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/containrrr/watchtower/main/README.md: '### ⚠️ This project is no longer maintained. See https://github.com/containrrr/watchtower/discussions/2135'. The github.com repo page says 'archived by the owner on Dec 17, 2025. It is now read-only.' Discussion #2135 'Goodbye containrrr/watchtower!' is dated 2025-12-17T14:42:13Z and says 'A few of the active forks I've looked at are full of AI slop and while they might work, I wouldn't advice using any of them.' releases/latest redirects to v1.7.1, datetime 2023-11-11T18:48:09Z. Issue #2126, opened 2025-11-14 on Docker 29.0.0: 'Error response from daemon: client version 1.25 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.44, please upgrade your client to a newer version'. watchtower internal/flags/flags.go has 'const DockerAPIMinVersion string = "1.25"', 'viper.SetDefault("DOCKER_API_VERSION", DockerAPIMinVersion)' and an 'api-version' flag read from DOCKER_API_VERSION. https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/29.md, section 29.3.0 (2026-03-05): 'Lower minimum API version from v1.44 to v1.40 (Docker 19.03). moby/moby#52067'. https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/service/create.md lists '--update-failure-action (pause, continue, rollback)' and has no device option.

missed: Docker has a supported route to a host-side post-stop GPIO reset that works with restart policies, so it does not need a systemd wrapper. CDI has been on by default since Docker 28.2.0. A CDI spec in /etc/cdi can inject /dev/gpiochip* and declare an OCI poststop hook (e.g. pinctrl/gpioset driving BCM 22/23 HIGH = relays off). dockerd deletes the task on every container exit (monitor.go tsk.Delete), and runc destroy() then runs the poststop hooks on the host. This could make 'Docker + restart policy' meet NFR-003 without fighting Docker's advice against process managers. It is unverified on a Pi and has three limits. Hook failures do not block anything. The hook only runs when dockerd/containerd handle the exit. It does not cover a dockerd crash with live-restore. A hardware test (kill -9 inside the container, then check the pin levels) is required before relying on it.

If systemd supervises Docker, it supervises the docker CLI client, not the container. The container process is a child of containerd-shim and sits in Docker's own cgroup scope: the systemd cgroup driver is the default on cgroup v2 ('systemd is used on cgroup v2 hosts with systemd available', dockerd reference), and docker.service has Delegate=yes/KillMode=process. `docker run` forwards SIGTERM (--sig-proxy default true), but if the CLI is SIGKILLed or crashes, the container keeps running and holding the GPIO lines. systemd then runs ExecStopPost and restarts the unit while the old container still drives the relays, and the restart fails on the name clash. A safe unit therefore needs at least ExecStartPre=-docker rm -f <name>, ExecStop=docker stop <name>, restart policy 'no', and an ExecStopPost reset that cannot race a live container. Docker's own docs suggest `docker start`-style commands for process managers.

Every apt upgrade of docker-ce restarts dockerd (the postinst 'restart' action, verified in the 29.8.2 .deb), which stops the container mid-brew unless live-restore is on, and live-restore does not cover major upgrades. Docker deployments therefore need `apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io`, or engine upgrades limited to times when no brew is loaded. This applies to both Docker variants (restart policy and systemd-wrapped).

docker.service itself has StartLimitBurst=3 within StartLimitIntervalSec=60. If dockerd fails to start three times in 60 s (e.g. a corrupt /var/lib/docker after power loss on an SD card), systemd stops retrying and the controller container never starts. This is an extra failure mode for NFR-023 that a native unit does not have.

On 32-bit Pi OS Bookworm, the raspbian repo (get.docker.com's default there) is stuck at containerd.io 2.2.1 (2026-01-02), while Docker's Debian repo has 2.3.6. So that path misses containerd/runc security fixes too, not only engine updates. For 32-bit Bookworm, use Docker's Debian armhf repo or move to Trixie. The Pi OS install page still shows templated '29.8.2 ~raspbian' version strings that do not exist in that repo.

Boot delay under Docker is bounded, not open-ended: docker.service only Wants= network-online.target. With NetworkManager (Pi OS), NetworkManager-wait-online waits up to NM_ONLINE_TIMEOUT=60 s when no network is available, so without Wi-Fi the controller container may start about a minute later than a native unit. Meanwhile the relay pins stay at their boot defaults, which makes the config.txt gpio= safe-state line (SAFE-02) more important for Docker modes.
